set.explanation: Baseline work-up of newly diagnosed hypertension looks for target-organ damage, overall cardiovascular risk and clues to a secondary cause: urea and electrolytes with eGFR, urine albumin:creatinine ratio and dipstick for haematuria, HbA1c or glucose, a lipid profile, a 12-lead ECG (left ventricular hypertrophy) and fundoscopy. CT aortography is not a routine test; it is reserved for suspected aortic dissection, aneurysm or coarctation when there is a specific clinical clue such as radiofemoral delay or unequal arm pressures.

set.stem: On routine examination a patient with hypertension has a blood pressure of 165/105 mmHg. According to the European (ESH/ESC) and British Hypertension Society classification, this is:
set.explanation: In the ESH/ESC (and former British Hypertension Society) grading, high-normal is 130–139/85–89 mmHg, grade 1 is 140–159/90–99 mmHg, grade 2 is 160–179/100–109 mmHg and grade 3 is ≥180/≥110 mmHg. When systolic and diastolic values fall in different grades the higher grade applies; here both 165 and 105 mmHg fall in grade 2. The diagnosis should still be confirmed with repeated clinic readings or ambulatory/home monitoring before treatment decisions are made.

why: Same idea and level as htn-0004 (beta-blockers are not first-line antihypertensives); htn-0004 is better constructed (nicardipine is an odd oral first-line example)

set.explanation: Current NICE (NG136) and ESC guidance start treatment with an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic (indapamide, chlortalidone), increasingly as a single-pill combination. Beta-blockers are less effective at preventing stroke and have more metabolic adverse effects, so they are not routine first-line therapy for uncomplicated hypertension. They are used when there is a compelling indication such as angina, previous myocardial infarction, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or rate control of atrial fibrillation.

Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) causes cortisol and aldosterone deficiency, leading to sodium loss, hypovolaemia and hypotension, often postural. Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) is the commonest endocrine cause of hypertension; acromegaly raises blood pressure through GH/IGF-1-driven sodium retention; and congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 11β-hydroxylase or 17α-hydroxylase deficiency causes hypertension through excess 11-deoxycorticosterone. Other endocrine causes include Cushing's syndrome, phaeochromocytoma and primary hyperparathyroidism.

why: Same question as 39 Blocks htn-0004 (beta-blockers are not first-line antihypertensives)
Reprint of htn-0006 in the same Formative bank (beta-blockers not first-line); survivor is htn-0004

set.stem: A 45-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus is reviewed in the diabetes clinic. Her blood pressure was 145/95 mmHg and lisinopril was started. Baseline blood tests showed potassium 4.5 mmol/L, creatinine 159 µmol/L (1.8 mg/dL) and eGFR 47 mL/min/1.73 m². Three months later, potassium is 4.9 mmol/L, creatinine 177 µmol/L (2.0 mg/dL) and eGFR 44 mL/min/1.73 m². What is the most appropriate course of action?
set.explanation: A small rise in creatinine is expected after starting an ACE inhibitor because efferent arteriolar dilatation lowers glomerular filtration pressure. NICE advises continuing the drug if creatinine rises by less than 30% (or eGFR falls by less than 25%) and potassium stays below 6.0 mmol/L; here creatinine has risen by about 11% and eGFR by about 6%, so no change is needed beyond routine monitoring. Stopping and investigating for renal artery stenosis is warranted only with a larger rise, and reducing the dose or switching would sacrifice the renoprotective benefit in diabetes.

set.stem: A 42-year-old man with known hypertension who ran out of his medication presents with a blood pressure of 230/140 mmHg, severe headache, dizziness and blurred optic disc margins (papilloedema) on fundoscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: A hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension (usually ≥180/120 mmHg) with acute target-organ damage — here papilloedema (grade 4 retinopathy), i.e. malignant (accelerated) hypertension, which the ESC classifies as a hypertensive emergency. Hypertensive urgency is equally high pressure without acute organ damage and is managed with oral agents; white-coat and isolated systolic hypertension do not fit, and nothing here suggests a secondary cause. He needs admission to a monitored bed and controlled intravenous blood pressure reduction.

why: 'Malignant hypertension' replaced by 'Hypertensive urgency': malignant hypertension with papilloedema is itself a hypertensive emergency, so two options were correct
The same Log Book case asks the same 'label the hypertensive state' question twice; this copy also lacked its scenario

set.stem: A 42-year-old man with known hypertension who ran out of his medication presents with a blood pressure of 230/140 mmHg, severe headache, dizziness and papilloedema on fundoscopy. Which of the following is an appropriate first-line antihypertensive in this situation?
set.explanation: A hypertensive emergency needs a titratable intravenous drug in a monitored setting, and of these options only intravenous nitroprusside fits. For malignant hypertension the ESC suggests IV labetalol or nicardipine first, with nitroprusside or urapidil as alternatives, lowering mean arterial pressure by no more than 20–25% over the first several hours to avoid cerebral, coronary and renal hypoperfusion. Oral or sublingual agents (amlodipine, captopril, lisinopril) act too slowly or unpredictably and are used for hypertensive urgency or once the patient is stable; thiazides have no role in acute control.

why: Stem made self-contained (scenario was in a preceding item); impossible option 'intramuscular enalaprilat' replaced by oral bendroflumethiazide

set.stem: A 56-year-old man presents with headache. On auscultation he has a loud second heart sound. Which of the following could explain this finding?
set.explanation: Systemic hypertension raises aortic diastolic pressure, so the aortic valve closes more forcefully and A2 (and hence S2) becomes loud, sometimes with a ringing 'tambour' quality. Aortic incompetence tends to soften A2, mitral incompetence gives a soft S1 with a pansystolic murmur, and a mechanical mitral valve produces a crisp metallic closing click with S1 rather than a loud S2. Postural hypotension does not alter the heart sounds.

set.stem: A 35-year-old executive has a reproducible blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg and is referred to clinic to look for an underlying cause. What is the commonest cause of secondary hypertension?
set.explanation: Renal disease — parenchymal disease (diabetic nephropathy, glomerulonephritis, polycystic kidney disease) together with renovascular disease — accounts for the largest share of secondary hypertension, which overall causes about 5–10% of cases. Primary aldosteronism is the commonest endocrine cause and should be screened for with an aldosterone:renin ratio in young or resistant hypertensives, whereas Cushing's syndrome, phaeochromocytoma, congenital adrenal hyperplasia and thyrotoxicosis are much rarer. In a young woman, fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal arteries should also be considered.

why: Conn's syndrome replaced by Cushing's syndrome: recent prevalence data make primary aldosteronism a defensible rival answer to renal disease

set.stem: A 60-year-old man is referred by his family doctor because his blood pressure remains uncontrolled despite four drugs, and a secondary cause is suspected. What is the commonest cause of poorly controlled hypertension?
set.explanation: Apparent treatment resistance is most often pseudo-resistance: poor adherence (found in up to half of such patients on drug-level testing), white-coat effect, faulty measurement technique or interfering substances such as NSAIDs, alcohol and high salt intake. These should be excluded — with ambulatory monitoring and an adherence assessment — before investigating secondary causes. Among true secondary causes in resistant hypertension, primary aldosteronism is the commonest, whereas glucocorticoid-suppressible hyperaldosteronism and primary hyper-reninaemia are rare.

set.stem: All of the following statements regarding the epidemiology of hypertension are true EXCEPT:
options: Among people aged 60 years or older, average systolic blood pressure is higher in women than in men
Diastolic blood pressure increases steadily with age throughout life
Systolic blood pressure continues to rise with age throughout adult life
In industrialised nations, blood pressure rises steadily during the first two decades of life
Worldwide, around one-third of adults aged 30–79 years have hypertension
set.explanation: Systolic pressure rises steadily throughout life, whereas diastolic pressure rises until about 50–60 years and then plateaus or falls as the large arteries stiffen, which is why isolated systolic hypertension predominates in older people. Blood pressure rises through childhood and adolescence in industrialised populations, older women have higher average systolic pressure than men, and WHO estimates that about 1.3 billion adults aged 30–79 years (roughly a third) have hypertension.

why: US-specific and dated distractors (Mexican American prevalence; '30% of US adults') replaced by current global facts; key unchanged

set.explanation: Cardiac disease — coronary heart disease, left ventricular hypertrophy with heart failure and arrhythmias — is the most common cause of death in people with hypertension. Stroke is the complication most tightly linked to blood pressure level and a major cause of disability, while hypertensive nephrosclerosis contributes to chronic kidney disease but causes fewer deaths. A 10 mmHg fall in systolic pressure reduces coronary events by about a fifth and stroke and heart failure by about a quarter.

set.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had hypertension that is difficult to control since the age of 26 years, requiring increasing doses of medication. Her current regimen is labetalol 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 40 mg once daily, clonidine 0.1 mg twice daily and amlodipine 5 mg once daily. She appears well; blood pressure is 168/100 mmHg and heart rate 84 bpm. Cardiac examination is unremarkable, peripheral pulses are good and there is no oedema. There is no hirsutism, abnormal fat distribution or genital abnormality. Serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/L, bicarbonate 32 mmol/L and fasting glucose 6.3 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
set.explanation: Resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis — despite an ACE inhibitor, which should raise potassium — points to mineralocorticoid excess, most often primary aldosteronism (Conn's syndrome, from an adenoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia). Cushing's syndrome is unlikely without its physical features, congenital adrenal hyperplasia usually causes virilisation or genital abnormalities, and phaeochromocytoma typically causes paroxysmal symptoms without hypokalaemia. Fibromuscular dysplasia can cause hypokalaemia through secondary hyperaldosteronism, but renin would then be high; the next step is an aldosterone:renin ratio.

set.stem: A 28-year-old woman has resistant hypertension despite four antihypertensive drugs. She has no cushingoid features. Serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/L and bicarbonate 32 mmol/L. What is the best initial test to establish the diagnosis?
set.explanation: The plasma aldosterone:renin ratio is the recommended screening test for primary aldosteronism: high aldosterone with suppressed renin gives a raised ratio. Hypokalaemia should be corrected first and interfering drugs (mineralocorticoid antagonists, diuretics, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors) adjusted where possible; a positive screen is confirmed by saline infusion or fludrocortisone suppression testing, then adrenal CT and adrenal vein sampling distinguish adenoma from bilateral hyperplasia. Urinary metanephrines test for phaeochromocytoma, urinary free cortisol for Cushing's syndrome, and renal vein renin or renal artery imaging for renovascular disease.

set.stem: A 65-year-old engineer who never sees a doctor and takes no medications is brought to the emergency department with a headache that has worsened over the past day and confusion that began an hour ago. Blood pressure is 230/140 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm and oxygen saturation 95%. He moves all limbs equally and has no cranial nerve deficit but is clearly delirious. The apex beat is forceful and displaced with an S4 gallop; the lungs are clear. Creatinine is 212 µmol/L (2.4 mg/dL), urine shows 2+ protein and haematuria, haematocrit is 0.32 with a normal platelet count, and the blood film shows schistocytes. Urgent brain MRI shows old microvascular changes but no acute infarct or haemorrhage. Which is the most reasonable approach to his blood pressure?
options: Intravenous labetalol 20 mg followed by a continuous infusion, aiming for a mean arterial pressure of about 125 mmHg in the first hour
set.explanation: This is malignant hypertension with encephalopathy, acute kidney injury and microangiopathic haemolysis — a hypertensive emergency needing a titratable intravenous agent (labetalol, nicardipine or nitroprusside) in a high-dependency setting. His mean arterial pressure is about 170 mmHg, so a target of about 125 mmHg is the recommended fall of no more than 20–25% in the first hour; faster reduction risks cerebral and renal ischaemia because autoregulation is reset upwards. Oral clonidine, lisinopril and immediate-release nifedipine give slow or unpredictable (sometimes precipitous) falls, and plasma exchange is for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, made unlikely here by the normal platelet count.

options: Because of tight precapillary regulation, the glomerular capillary endothelium is relatively shielded from pressure injury
Renal cortical blood flow is less than renal medullary blood flow, and together with the high metabolic needs of the cortex this leaves the cortex bordering on hypoxia
Renal perfusion is tightly matched to the metabolic needs of the kidney
Urinary albumin excretion predicts systemic atherosclerotic events and can appear years before clinical atherosclerotic disease
Venous blood returning from the renal cortex has a lower oxygen content than venous blood returning from the renal medulla
set.explanation: Albuminuria reflects generalised endothelial dysfunction and predicts cardiovascular events and mortality, often years before clinical atherosclerotic disease, which is why a urine albumin:creatinine ratio is part of the hypertension work-up. The kidneys receive about 20% of cardiac output — far more than their metabolic needs, because the flow serves filtration — and most goes to the cortex; the medulla receives little flow and borders on hypoxia, so cortical venous blood is the more oxygen-rich. Glomerular capillaries operate at high pressure and are directly exposed to systemic hypertension, especially when autoregulation fails.

Reduced renal perfusion stimulates renin release, so early renovascular hypertension is renin–angiotensin-dependent with raised plasma renin; later, sodium retention and contralateral kidney changes can normalise renin, and renin activity does not reliably predict response to revascularisation or drugs. A haemodynamically significant stenosis on Doppler shows increased, not reduced, peak systolic velocity. Fibromuscular dysplasia is found in about 3–6% of normotensive potential kidney donors and usually presents as hypertension in young to middle-aged women with preserved renal function.

set.stem: A man has been diagnosed with essential hypertension by his GP and is about to start treatment. Which of the following statements about the treatment of essential hypertension is true?
options: Alpha-blockers such as prazosin rarely cause postural hypotension
Patients of African-Caribbean origin respond well to ACE inhibitor monotherapy
ACE inhibitors are safe in bilateral renal artery stenosis
Treatment with bendroflumethiazide may cause hypokalaemia
ACE inhibitors commonly cause ankle swelling
set.explanation: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics increase sodium delivery to the collecting duct, promoting potassium loss and causing hypokalaemia (as well as hyponatraemia, hyperuricaemia/gout and hyperglycaemia). Prazosin and other alpha-blockers characteristically cause first-dose postural hypotension; people of Black African or African-Caribbean origin respond less well to ACE inhibitor monotherapy, so a calcium-channel blocker is preferred; and ACE inhibitors can precipitate acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis. Ankle swelling is typical of dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, not ACE inhibitors.

why: Distractor on unilateral renal artery stenosis changed to bilateral: ACE inhibitors are used (with monitoring) for unilateral stenosis, so the original statement was arguably true

set.stem: A 50-year-old man has a persistently raised blood pressure of about 185/110 mmHg. He has had headaches for a few weeks but is otherwise well. His ECG shows increased QRS voltages with ST depression in the left ventricular leads, and fundoscopy shows arteriovenous nipping without haemorrhages or papilloedema. What is the most appropriate management?
set.explanation: He has severe (grade 3) hypertension with established target-organ damage — left ventricular hypertrophy with strain and grade 2 retinopathy — but no acute features such as papilloedema, retinal haemorrhages, encephalopathy or acute kidney injury. In this situation oral treatment should be started straight away, without waiting for ambulatory monitoring, with review within days; admission and intravenous therapy are reserved for hypertensive emergencies. Lifestyle advice alone or waiting 2 months leaves him at high short-term risk, and an exercise test is not the priority.

set.stem: A 50-year-old white man sees his GP for a blood pressure check, having recently been diagnosed with essential hypertension. His only other condition is type 2 diabetes mellitus without end-organ damage, well controlled on oral hypoglycaemic agents. His blood pressure has remained about 145/90 mmHg despite 3 months of diet and exercise. Which is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive?
set.explanation: In type 2 diabetes NICE recommends an ACE inhibitor as step 1 whatever the patient's age (an ARB if an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated, or in people of Black African or African-Caribbean origin), because renin–angiotensin blockade reduces albuminuria and slows diabetic kidney disease. A calcium-channel blocker or thiazide-like diuretic is added at step 2, while beta-blockers and alpha-blockers such as doxazosin are not first-line agents. The clinic target is below 140/90 mmHg (about 130/80 mmHg in ESC/ADA guidance).

why: Losartan replaced by doxazosin: an ARB is also listed first line in diabetes, so two options were correct

set.explanation: Severe hypertension without acute target-organ damage (hypertensive urgency) should be lowered gradually over hours to days with oral agents. Abrupt reduction in the emergency department — for example with intravenous drugs or immediate-release nifedipine — can precipitate stroke or myocardial or renal ischaemia, because autoregulation is shifted to higher pressures in chronic hypertension. Appropriate care is a short period of observation, restarting or adjusting oral treatment, checking adherence and community follow-up within 1–2 days.

About 90–95% of hypertension is primary (essential), with no single identifiable cause; it results from an interplay of genetic predisposition, age-related arterial stiffening, salt intake, obesity, alcohol and inactivity. Secondary causes such as polycystic kidney disease, coarctation of the aorta, renin-secreting tumours and drugs like the combined oral contraceptive account for only 5–10% of cases, but should be sought in young patients, in resistant hypertension or when there are suggestive clues.

why: Same idea and level as htn-0024 (hypertension with type 2 diabetes: start an ACE inhibitor); weaker stem based on a single reading

set.explanation: In the Keith–Wagener–Barker classification, grade 1 is arteriolar narrowing and silver-wiring, grade 2 adds arteriovenous nipping, grade 3 adds flame-shaped haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots, and grade 4 adds papilloedema; there is no grade 5. Grade 3–4 changes indicate severe hypertension, and retinal haemorrhages or papilloedema with very high blood pressure should prompt same-day specialist assessment for accelerated hypertension.

set.stem: A 55-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with lethargy and a blood pressure of 250/150 mmHg. Her family say she complained of severe headache and visual disturbance earlier in the day. She has a history of asthma but no known kidney disease. Fundoscopy shows retinal haemorrhages. Which of the following is the best approach?
set.explanation: This is a hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy, requiring a monitored bed and a titratable intravenous agent. Labetalol is often first choice but, as a non-selective beta-blocker, is contraindicated in asthma, so a nitroprusside infusion (or nicardipine/clevidipine where available) is preferred, lowering mean arterial pressure by no more than about 25% in the first hour. Oral clonidine is too slow and unpredictable, sublingual nifedipine causes precipitous falls with stroke and myocardial ischaemia, and a loop diuretic is not primary therapy because these patients are often volume-depleted.

set.stem: A 50-year-old construction worker continues to have a blood pressure of 160/95 mmHg even after a third agent is added to his antihypertensive regimen. Physical examination is normal, electrolytes are normal and he takes no over-the-counter medications. Which of the following is the best next step?
set.explanation: Before labelling hypertension as resistant, pseudo-resistance must be excluded: non-adherence is the commonest cause and can be assessed with a pill count, prescription records or drug-level testing, alongside ambulatory monitoring to confirm true blood pressure. Salt and alcohol intake, NSAIDs and obstructive sleep apnoea should also be reviewed. Screening for secondary causes (primary aldosteronism, renovascular disease, Cushing's syndrome, coarctation) follows only when resistance is genuine or there are specific clues, and normal electrolytes and examination make these less likely.

set.stem: You see a 45-year-old woman with diabetes mellitus for the first time in clinic. Her systolic blood pressure was above 140 mmHg at each of her last two clinic appointments, home blood pressure monitoring over the past week averaged 150/90 mmHg, and her clinic blood pressure today is 164/92 mmHg. What is the best next step in her blood pressure management?
options: Ask her to keep a written record of her home blood pressure and bring it to a return appointment
Advise a heart-healthy, low-sodium diet and refer her to a dietitian
Prescribe an ACE inhibitor in addition to a heart-healthy diet
Prescribe a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker in addition to a heart-healthy diet
Arrange an echocardiogram to assess for end-organ damage
set.explanation: Hypertension is confirmed by raised clinic readings on separate occasions plus a home average above 135/85 mmHg, and in diabetes drug treatment should start alongside lifestyle advice rather than lifestyle measures alone. An ACE inhibitor (or ARB) is preferred in diabetes because it reduces albuminuria and slows nephropathy; a calcium-channel blocker is an alternative or add-on rather than the preferred first agent. Echocardiography is not routine — an ECG, urine albumin:creatinine ratio, renal function and fundoscopy assess target-organ damage.

why: Confirmatory home readings added: without them, further out-of-office monitoring (first option) was defensible under NICE

set.stem: A 45-year-old man with hypertension attends his GP for review. His last clinic reading was 156/80 mmHg, and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring shows a daytime average of 138/85 mmHg. He is already taking the maximum dose of ramipril. Which agent would be most appropriate to add?
set.explanation: His daytime ambulatory average of 138/85 mmHg is above the NICE target (below 135/85 mmHg for people under 80), so step 2 treatment is needed: add a calcium-channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic such as indapamide to the ACE inhibitor. Spironolactone (if potassium ≤4.5 mmol/L) or an alpha- or beta-blocker (if potassium >4.5 mmol/L) are step 4 options for resistant hypertension, and bisoprolol is otherwise reserved for compelling indications. Verapamil, a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker, is not used for hypertension alone.

set.stem: Which one of the following statements regarding hypertension in pregnancy is NOT correct?
options: A rise above booking readings of more than 30 mmHg systolic or 15 mmHg diastolic suggests hypertension
Pre-eclampsia occurs in around 5% of pregnancies
A urine dipstick showing protein + is consistent with gestational hypertension
A rise in blood pressure before 20 weeks suggests pre-existing hypertension
In gestational hypertension the blood pressure rises in the second half of pregnancy
set.explanation: Gestational hypertension is new hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) after 20 weeks without significant proteinuria; new hypertension with proteinuria (urine protein:creatinine ratio ≥30 mg/mmol) or other maternal organ dysfunction defines pre-eclampsia, so proteinuria is not consistent with simple gestational hypertension. Hypertension before 20 weeks suggests chronic (pre-existing) hypertension, pre-eclampsia complicates about 2–8% of pregnancies, and a rise of more than 30/15 mmHg above booking values is an older criterion still used to flag concern. Labetalol is first-line treatment, with nifedipine or methyldopa as alternatives.
